$comment: The registry of controls this repository claims to have, and the probe that proves each claim.
version: a document may not assert that a control is configured unless a probe named here
reads that configuration from its own source of truth. Prose is a claim; a probe is evidence.
JSON rather than YAML on purpose. This repo has no YAML parser dependency, so a YAML
registry would need a hand-written one — and a hand-written parser that silently matches
nothing is exactly the failure this registry exists to catch. A registry whose own reader
could quietly return an empty set would be the joke writing itself.
src/tests/unit/control-registry.test.ts enforces the invariants: every probe path exists and
is wired into the workflow named here, every adr path exists, nothing may claim
status 'configured' without a scheduled probe, and every control-shaped ADR has an entry.

controls.claims: main requires the three CI check runs, up to date with main, through a pull request, with no bypass actor, before a pull request can merge
controls.knownLimit: Configured since 2026-10-03, on two observations recorded in docs/runbooks/main-ruleset.md: the 05:00 UTC read-back of ruleset 24077858 judged conclusive, and the 07:56 UTC v2 canary #98 read `denied` and closed unmerged. The probe reads; it cannot change protection. What keeps asking afterwards is this probe, six-hourly in control-audit.yml, and how much it sees depends on its token. With CONTROL_AUDIT_TOKEN (administration read) it sees the classic layer and the ruleset's bypass list, so a removed context, a dropped strict or pull-request rule, an added bypass actor or a deleted ruleset each disagree with `configured`: the step exits 1, and an absent gate also opens the merge-gate-unenforced issue. Without that token (the 2026-10-03 audit read `unevaluable`, so it is either unset or lacks administration read; the secret list is not readable from an agent session), classic protection answers 403 and the bypass list is not returned, so the probe reads `unevaluable` and exits 0. The one regression it still reports then is a required context that no job publishes; every other regression stays invisible until the token is set or someone reads the ruleset. The canary's proof holds for the ruleset version it ran against (updated_at 2026-10-03T04:59:37Z), and Step 3 is re-run after any change. merge_group is untested, because there is no merge queue. Code-owner review is reported, never required: with one human maintainer it deadlocks, because GitHub blocks self-approval.
controls.humanAction: Add, or fix, the CONTROL_AUDIT_TOKEN repository secret: a fine-grained token, administration read on this repository only, entered by the owner and never shown to an agent. Without it the six-hourly probe cannot see a regression (knownLimit). After any change to ruleset 24077858, read it back (docs/runbooks/main-ruleset.md, step 2) and, with the owner's permission, re-run the v2 canary (step 3). When editing its contexts, never type `verify` or `e2e`: those are job IDs and would register two contexts nothing reports, blocking every PR permanently. Run `pnpm exec vitest run required-checks-contract` first.

controls.claims: the five production-smoke secrets are scoped to the production-readonly environment, not to the repository
controls.humanAction: GitHub → Settings → Environments → production-readonly: put the five secrets there and set the variable SMOKE_SECRETS_SOURCE=environment. Never set that marker at repository scope — it is what distinguishes isolated from merely green.
controls.knownLimit: A convention, not an enforcement. GitHub gives a job no way to ask where a secret came from, so setting the marker at repository scope defeats it. Recorded rather than overclaimed — ADR 006.
controls.acceptedWhy: Restated 2026-09-15 by the defects review, and corrected: the previous reason named the wrong blocker. Issue #24 is that SHOPIFY_ADMIN_ACCESS_TOKEN holds a token of the wrong kind, which is a different fact from this control, and citing it here made an unmet isolation requirement read as a downstream consequence of a credential problem. This control is about scope, not validity: the five smoke secrets must sit on the production-readonly GitHub Environment with the SMOKE_SECRETS_SOURCE=environment marker, because this repository is public and forkable and repository-scoped secrets are readable by every workflow. Correcting the token would not close this gap; moving the secrets would, whatever the token holds. It stays accepted because both are GitHub console actions nobody in CI can perform, and preflight-secrets.mjs asserts the marker so the difference between isolated and merely green stays observable.

controls.claims: the deployed site serves every catalogue handle, 404s the ones it does not hold, references no Shopify host, and emits no commerce semantics
controls.humanAction: None. Wired into production-smoke.yml on 2026-09-20 as the `Browse-only catalogue` step, replacing `verify-production.mjs` — whose seventeen checks all needed a Shopify credential and whose central discriminator had inverted, since a live site serving the bundled catalogue is now correct. This probe needs nothing: PRODUCTION_SITE_URL when set, otherwise the apex read out of src/config/site.ts. It therefore carries no capability gate and cannot be skipped by an empty secret, which is what un-darkens this tier without the console action issue #81 was otherwise waiting on. Measured clean against a local production build before wiring: 24 responses against 17 catalogue handles. The first scheduled run against production, #159 on 2026-09-20T20:30Z, reported 25 findings against a site that was serving the catalogue correctly: the apex answers 307 and hands every path to the www host. That was a defect in this probe, not in the site — see knownLimit and the 2026-09-21 fix, which collapses a whole-host redirect into one finding and re-anchors the sweep one hop within the same registrable domain.
controls.knownLimit: Two. It reads expected handles from the *filenames* in src/content/catalog/products/ rather than from parsed records, because it is dependency-free .mjs and cannot import the TypeScript reader — that shortcut is licensed only by catalog-content.test.ts asserting every file is named after the handle inside it, and removing that assertion silently points this probe at URLs with no records behind them. And it judges what a response *contains*: a page that omits a price because the data is missing looks identical to one that omits it because the decommission removed the field. Third, since 2026-09-21 it will follow **one** redirect from the base URL, and only to a host sharing the same last two labels. That is a deliberate widening of what it will measure and a bounded one: the redirect is still reported as `canonical-host-redirects`, the run is still red, and the output names which origin the catalogue findings describe. A redirect leaving the brand's own domain is never followed — a probe that chases one reports some other origin's health as ours. `registrableDomain` compares the last two labels rather than consulting a public-suffix list, which would call two unrelated sites on a multi-label suffix like `co.uk` the same site; this repository owns one name and never sees one.
controls.acceptedWhy: **The 2026-09-20 acceptance expired on its own terms and is not renewed for the same reason.** It read, in full: accepted on the day it was written, for one scheduled-run cycle rather than indefinitely. The probe is complete and its decision is covered by 32 fixture-driven assertions; what is missing is a site for it to pass against. Run against the current deployment it returns `findings` with 52 entries, every one of them true: 17 products x 3 surviving commerce markers (Offer JSON-LD, a price field, a schema.org availability claim), plus /products/<unknown> answering 200 rather than 404. Those are WS-5's and WS-4's work respectively. Scheduling a check that cannot pass until two other workstreams land trains the reader to ignore it, which is precisely what ADR 011 records costing this repository a month of unread escalations. The acceptance expires when WS-4 and WS-5 merge; probe-accepted-gap.mjs will say so if they have not. Both merged in PR #83 on 2026-09-20, and the 52 findings that acceptance described are gone — the commerce markers with WS-5, the soft 404 with WS-4's `dynamicParams = false`. What replaces it is narrower and is about a hostname rather than about this repository: the probe reports one true finding, `canonical-host-redirects`, and will keep reporting it until someone clears the redirect on the apex in Vercel. That is a console action nobody in CI can perform, it is tracked as the `domain-unbound` issue the canonical-domain probe opens, and the check goes green the moment it is done. Nothing in this repository can close it, which is what distinguishes it from the gap it replaces.

controls.claims: no commerce identifier, package, route or document can enter this repository without being classified in COMMERCE-ELIMINATION-CONTRACT.md or owned by a row in docs/commerce-dependency-register.md; every register row and every whole-file exemption declares exactly the identifiers it excuses, reconciled as sets in both directions
controls.knownLimit: Three limits, each measured, two of them narrowed on 2026-09-26 (ADR 037). (1) The position split is a hand-written lexer — strings, templates with nested `${}`, regex literals, JSX — not a parser. commerce-lexer-differential.test.ts checks it line by line against the TypeScript compiler's own comment ranges on every tracked JS/TS file and fails on any disagreement, so its coverage is measured for the C family; the old lexer misread 661 lines in 67 files, and one misread hid an absolute finding, which is why 'weakens a finding rather than inventing one' was never the safe direction for a prohibition scanner. The `#` family (YAML, shell, dotenv) has no second implementation and is asserted by fixtures only; regex-versus-division is decided from the previous token, so `if (x) /re/` is outside it — the differential would name the file. (2) It reads tracked text files, so it cannot see a dependency reached at runtime through a generated path, an env var assembled from fragments, or anything untracked; what the build emits is scripts/scan-build-artifacts.mjs's question (control build-artifact-boundary). (3) `negative-control` and `specification` rows now declare in §4 `Carries` the exact identifiers their exemption covers, held as a set in both directions; what remains unseen is a further occurrence of an already-carried identifier inside such a file, and anything in `historical` files, which stay whole-file exempt by design.

controls.claims: something asks, every six hours, whether healthyjewellery.com and its www host both reach this project's production deployment on the same commit — and reports the answer whatever it is
controls.knownLimit: Three limits, all deliberate. First, nothing watches control-audit.yml, so if that workflow stops executing this check goes silent and its silence is indistinguishable from an all-clear — the same shape control-acceptance-freshness records one tier up, and the weekly human backstop is what covers it. Second, this probe follows a redirect chain and `verify-browse-only.mjs` does not, so for one redirect the two report different numbers by design — this one names the status of the hop that redirected (`redirectStatus`), the browse-only probe names the only status it has, which is the immediate one. They do not disagree; they answer different questions. Conflating the two put “answers 200 and redirects” into issue #84 on 2026-09-25, where the 200 came from the end of the chain and the sentence described something that cannot happen. Third, this entry claims that something *asks*, not that the domain is currently bound: the live verdict is the probe's output, in canonical-domain.json and in one domain-unbound issue, and is deliberately not copied into this file. A hand-edited registry holding a live fact is a second copy that drifts from the first, which is the shape ADR 018 exists to refuse.
controls.humanAction: None while this reads green. When it opens a domain-unbound issue, the action is in Vercel -> Project -> Settings -> Domains: both hostnames attached to this project and assigned to Production, with www permanently redirecting to the apex. **Read the finding code before acting.** `apex-redirected` means the redirect is installed on the wrong hostname and the fix is to clear it on the apex first, then add it on www — doing only the second half leaves a redirect loop. `www-not-redirected` means the redirect is simply missing. Until 2026-09-21 the first of those could not be reported at all and surfaced as the second, which reads as an instruction to change the hostname that is behaving correctly. Never change DNS at Shopify — docs/dns-domain-setup.md records why a ssl.com CAA record would block Vercel's own certificate renewal.

controls.claims: every record in src/content/catalog/** is parsed against its Zod schema before a single page is generated, and an invalid one fails the build
controls.knownLimit: The check runs because next.config.ts imports the reader, so it is one import away from silently not running at all — and before that import existed a malformed record passed `pnpm build` cleanly. catalog-content.test.ts reads next.config.ts back out and fails if the import or its call goes, and asserts manifest.ts uses relative paths, because Next's config loader ignores tsconfig path mappings and an alias anywhere in that graph would skip the check rather than fail it. It validates shape, never truth: a product whose description is accurate JSON and inaccurate metallurgy passes.

controls.claims: no module outside src/lib/catalog/** imports a raw record from src/content/catalog/**, by any import form
controls.knownLimit: Resolves imports through the TypeScript compiler API rather than scanning text, so a comment and a template literal are correctly not imports and a dynamic import correctly is — but it sees only static module edges. Content reached at runtime through fs, a fetch or a generated path is invisible to it, which is one reason manifest.ts uses static imports rather than a directory walk. It also walks src/ and e2e/ only: a new top-level source directory would be outside its sweep until added.

controls.claims: every deliberately-accepted control gap is re-decided within 30 days, and a person is told when one is not
controls.knownLimit: Nothing watches this probe. probe-ci-liveness.mjs watches ci.yml and probe-smoke-liveness.mjs watches production-smoke.yml, but no probe watches control-audit.yml — so if that workflow stops executing, this check goes silent and its silence is indistinguishable from an all-clear. That is the exact shape ADR 022 names, one tier up, and it is stated here rather than implied because an unstated limit is how the merge gate stayed dark for eleven runs. The weekly human backstop is what covers it today.
controls.humanAction: None while this reads green. When it opens a control-acceptance-stale issue, the action is to re-decide the named gap in docs/controls.json — either close it, or update acceptedSince and acceptedWhy to say it is still a deliberate choice. Never bump the date without re-reading the reason: that is the snooze this control exists to make visible.

controls.claims: every workflow runs its steps under pipefail, so a piped step cannot report success for a failing command
the 80% coverage thresholds in vitest.config.ts are evaluated by the merge gate and applied to every file, not merely declared over an average
controls.knownLimit: Scoped to src/lib and src/config on purpose — src/store was in that list until 2026-09-20 and the directory went with the cart, so the glob matched nothing while still reading as coverage of something that exists (ADR 035). The UI layer is covered by E2E, and e2e/COVERAGE.md is the compensating control for it. Within that scope the floor is now per-file with no glob exemptions: the aggregate form of this threshold hid five files below 80% behind a 91% total on 2026-09-15, customer/client.ts at 0% among them, which is what issue 14 of that review recorded and what perFile: true closed on 2026-09-18.

controls.claims: no workflow condition reads another step's result while silently also requiring that nothing earlier succeeded
one pnpm version resolves this lockfile, and the four CVE overrides cannot be removed without a test failing
controls.knownLimit: Covers this repository's declarations only. Dependabot resolves lockfiles on its own infrastructure and honours `packageManager`, but nothing here can prove it did — the evidence is that the regenerated lockfile still carries its `overrides:` block, which `--frozen-lockfile` checks on every run.

controls.claims: one declared Node version resolves this repository, and every workflow and Vercel read it from the same field
controls.knownLimit: Covers this repository's declarations only. Vercel reads `engines.node` from its own build image and nothing here can prove which patch it resolved — the guarantee is that it reads the same field, and the same major, as CI does. Playwright is deliberately outside this control: `ci.yml` derives the browser version from the installed `@playwright/test` package and keys its cache on it, so the lockfile is already that tool's single authority and a second declaration would be the regression.

controls.claims: neither package.json nor pnpm-lock.yaml carries a conflict marker or declares a key twice, and the manifest's ranges agree with the lockfile's, checked before the install that all of these break
controls.knownLimit: Four questions. Duplicate keys in package.json is the half nothing else asks: JSON permits them, JSON.parse takes the last occurrence silently, and on 2026-09-18 main carried five of them while every tool read one value from a file that stated two. Duplicate keys in pnpm-lock.yaml were left to pnpm until 2026-10-04 (ADR 031), and on 2026-10-03 this step printed two ticks above an install that died on ten of them (PR #101, ed7594a; ADR 046). They are now read by a scanner for the YAML subset pnpm writes, measured against the `yaml` package on the real lockfile and on 120 seeded mutations of it, which reports `unevaluable` (exit 2) on any construct outside that subset rather than `ok`. Conflict markers in either file are a finding, and no longer throw out of the probe. Manifest/lockfile divergence is already detected by `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`; this names it. It reads the root importer only, so a workspace package would be outside the range comparison, and it compares declared ranges rather than resolved versions. Detection only: the prevention is `.gitattributes` (`pnpm-lock.yaml merge=binary`), asserted as behaviour by a real three-way merge in the same test file. Whether GitHub's web conflict editor honours that attribute has not yet been observed on a live conflict.

controls.claims: no server function's trace ships repository files — source, tests, docs, scripts — unless a runtime read is named for it, and every file a function reads at runtime is in that function's trace
controls.knownLimit: Reads the `.nft.json` traces of the build CI just made, which are what Vercel packages each function from; it does not read Vercel's own output, so a platform-side packaging difference is outside it. Exits 2 when there are no traces to read, never 0 (ADR 020). The 'nothing missing' half could not be provoked on a real build: on 2026-10-04 four mutations of the share card's font path, `turbopackIgnore` among them, all left the fonts traced, because Turbopack folds constant paths and the trace pass follows partly unknown ones by wildcard. It is kept because that behaviour belongs to two tools, and a missing file fails only on Vercel. RUNTIME_READS is a hand-kept list; a new runtime read has to be added to it, which is the point.

controls.claims: a pull request cannot raise the major of next, react or react-dom without a written rationale in its description
controls.knownLimit: It reports; it does not block, because main has no branch protection and a red X sits beside a merge button anyone can still press. Registered as configured because the check itself runs and fails correctly — what is missing is the merge-gate control it would hang from, which is why that is its backstop rather than human:weekly. It also reads the package.json diff only: a major arriving through a transitive dependency, or through pnpm.overrides, is outside it. And `hasWrittenRationale` asks whether somebody wrote a paragraph under a heading, not whether the paragraph is any good — bounded coverage, stated rather than claimed (ADR 007). Until 2026-09-18 it read the description **frozen into the webhook payload** (`github.event.pull_request.body`), which made it unsatisfiable by the one action it demands: `pull_request` does not fire when a description is edited, and a re-run replays the original payload, so a `## Rationale` written in answer to this check's own failure message was invisible to it. The only sequence that cleared it was edit the description *then push a commit*. It now reads the body live from the pull requests API, so re-running the job is the remedy. What remains bounded is that nothing re-evaluates it automatically when the description changes — adding `pull_request: types: [edited]` would cancel the in-flight merge-gate run through ci.yml's ref-keyed concurrency group and replace it with a `skipped` indistinguishable from a pass, so the one click is the deliberate trade.
controls.humanAction: When this check fails and the rationale has since been written: re-run the `Dependency scope` job (Checks → Dependency scope → Re-run jobs). It reads the description live, so no commit on top is needed. If it still fails, the `## Rationale` heading is missing or the prose under it is under 40 characters — run `node scripts/audit-dependency-scope.mjs --base origin/main --json` to see exactly what it read and from where.

controls.claims: every consumer that installs from pnpm-lock.yaml passes --frozen-lockfile, so none of them can resolve around a lockfile the merge gate would reject
controls.knownLimit: Asserts what this repository declares, not what Vercel executes. A project-level Install Command set in the Vercel dashboard overrides vercel.json, and nothing here can read that — the same blind spot smoke-secret-isolation records for GitHub environment scoping. Verify it once in the dashboard and re-verify when the project is reconfigured; this check covers every other consumer, and covers the file a reviewer would read to answer the question.

controls.claims: a production-smoke failure repeating the same diagnosis escalates once instead of commenting every six hours, and the comparison that decides "same diagnosis" is a pure function with fixture tests rather than a string inside a YAML file
no github-script step in any workflow holds a decision: each is within a 45-line transport budget, and the four blocks that exceed it today are frozen at their current size and may not grow
every recorded decision that rests on a live premise has a detector that reports when the premise drifts
controls.knownLimit: One premise, and a different one. The six it held all lost their subject — five with the store's read path, SHOPIFY-API-VERSION with scripts/lib/api-version.mjs on 2026-09-26 — and a collector of nothing would write [] every run, which the reporter reads as 'all premises hold' (ADR 035). CHECKOUT-HOST-CNAME replaces them: checkout.<apex> still aliases the vendor's shops host, which is the premise WS-E's thirty-day retirement clock rests on. It is a DNS lookup with an NS control; a resolver that cannot answer is `unevaluable`, and then no drift file is written, so a timeout cannot close a real drift issue. It sees DNS only: it cannot tell who changed a record, and it is expected to drift — and be retired with the hostname — at the end of the WS-E clock.

controls.claims: the tests protecting 55 named invariants can still fail when those invariants are broken
controls.humanAction: None while this reads green. When it opens an `assertions-dead` issue, read the log in the issue body before acting — it carries two different findings. A *dead* sentinel means a test executed deliberately-broken code and stayed green, so the invariant it names is unprotected now and the fix is in that test. A probe that *refused to start*, or evaluated nothing, means the control is dark and says nothing either way about the suite; the fix is in the probe or the job around it. That reporting channel did not exist until 2026-09-21: the step was `continue-on-error` with its only trace a cell in a job summary, and it had been refusing to start on every scheduled run because the steps above it write untracked `.log` files that `git status --porcelain` counts as a dirty tree.
controls.knownLimit: Covers 33 declared sentinels, not the whole suite — and only the 31 with a vitest runner are evaluated on a schedule, because the two Playwright ones each need a production build. Both counts are reconciled against SENTINELS by sentinel-inventory.test.ts; this entry claimed seventeen until 2026-09-21, and the control-audit job summary claimed twelve, and nothing compared either to the thirteen that exist. A dead assertion outside that set is invisible to it, and the sentinel anchors are exact strings that a refactor will move — which is why the probe reports `unapplicable` loudly rather than skipping.

controls.claims: something has actually verified the live store within the last 26 hours, and that it has not just stopped doing so
controls.knownLimit: Cannot detect its own death. If control-audit.yml stops running, nothing reports that — the honest end of any monitoring chain, recorded rather than closed with a fourth watcher (ADR 006's precedent). It is also blind to a run whose step data the Actions API will not return, which it reports as unevaluable rather than as dark. The `stopped` verdict (ADR 033) needs one executing run inside the window to compare against, so a tier that was already dark when its secrets were removed reports `dark` and never `stopped` — correct, and it means the removal itself is not separately dated.

controls.claims: if CI runs on main stop evaluating the repository, an issue says so — a run that dies in setup reports every check as skipped, which from outside is indistinguishable from success
controls.knownLimit: Keys on the `Lint` step alone. A run whose lint executed has evaluated the repository, so an ordinary red build reads as `lit` — deliberately, because demanding that every check ran would alarm on each genuinely broken pull request and become a muted channel (ADR 011). It follows that a gate broken *after* lint, between lint and build, is not covered here; the merge gate's own red X carries that.

controls.claims: the hero copy card may occupy no more than 60% of the photograph it sits on
controls.knownLimit: The probe measures the card against the cap it reads from --hj-hero-card-max-ratio, so it cannot see the cap itself being raised: the card measures at most 0.514 of the photograph and 0.60 never binds, so at 0.98 nothing rendered moves and the ceiling moves with it (48 passed, 2026-10-02). The number is pinned instead by a doc-numeric-claims row that reads every declaration of the token in src (stylesheet rules, media queries, style-object keys, setProperty) against CLAUDE.md's stated 0.60, and the browser sentinel hero-card-measured proves the measurement fires on a card that outgrows its cap. That sentinel needs a production build and runs only under --with-e2e, never in the six-hourly audit.

controls.claims: every header control is reachable inside the viewport down to 320px
the product image tile is square, capped, and contained at every viewport
every route excused from E2E in e2e/COVERAGE.md names a test that exists and covers it
controls.knownLimit: Checks that a cited test exists and mentions the route, not that its assertions still mean anything — that is the fossil question, answered by control:assertion-liveness. Two of the nine exceptions were wrong the first time this ran: /api/version cited a file that tests the version-literal scan and never imports the route, leaving that route with no test at all, and /api/shopify cited an E2E spec that does not touch it.

controls.claims: every failure mode the code enumerates as a type is documented in docs/failure-modes.md with what detects it and what covers it
controls.knownLimit: Reconciles the seven registered union types in both directions; a failure mode with no type cannot be found by it. Those are listed in the document’s final table by hand, which is the part of the registry that can still go stale — a new un-enumerated degradation is invisible to this check in exactly the way an undocumented union member is not.

controls.claims: no two rate limiters share a Redis key prefix, so no two budgets silently merge
controls.knownLimit: Static by necessity, not by preference. With Upstash unconfigured — every test environment today — the in-memory fallback allocates a fresh Map per limiter and ignores the prefix entirely, so a collision is invisible to any test that drives requests through a route and appears only in production. A prefix built from a constant rather than written inline would also be missed, which is why the check asserts it found at least three limiters (there are four since /api/revalidate was deleted on 2026-09-25).

controls.claims: the unit suite runs under the same environment locally and in the merge gate, so a green local run is evidence about the gate
controls.knownLimit: Reconciles the declared environments, not the measured coverage. A module whose branch count depends on some *other* ambient difference — a locale, a TZ, a Node minor — is outside it. The real defence against that class is a test stubbing both arms, as config-env-branches.test.ts does for src/config; this control only removes the one difference that had already cost three red CI runs on 2026-09-18 while every local run was clean.

controls.claims: /api/contact reports success only when the mail provider returns a message id, and logs a refusal by error name and status code only, never the visitor's name, address or message
controls.knownLimit: The provider is mocked at the module boundary in the shape resend@6.28.1 returns ({ data, error }, never a throw on an API error — which is how the route answered { success: true } for refused sends until 2026-09-25: the old mock resolved { id } at the top level, so the suite could not see it). A future SDK major that changed the shape would pass these tests against a stale fixture. A successful send is not logged, so delivery volume is not observable from the logs.

controls.claims: no client IP is written to a rate-limit store: bucket keys are HMAC-SHA256 under RATE_LIMIT_KEY_SECRET, or SHA-256 under a versioned domain-separation prefix when that is unset, and /api/health reports which
controls.knownLimit: The in-memory fallback's map key is not observable from a test, so only the Upstash identifier is asserted directly; a mutation that keyed the map on the raw IP would stay green. 'unkeyed' is pseudonymous, not anonymous: the prefix is public and the IPv4 space is enumerable, which the privacy page says in those words. The Node-runtime premise the HMAC depends on is checked by an AST walk of importers that sees only a literal `export const runtime = 'edge'`.

controls.claims: the /api/analytics log line carries only an event that passes that event's own strict schema — a product, collection or material handle the catalogue publishes and counts no larger than the catalogue — and no free text at all: a search is recorded as the collections and metals it named, never the query
controls.knownLimit: Schema and event type are held equal in both directions by tsc (`EVENT_SCHEMAS` and `exact` in the route), so that half depends on the type-check running in the gate; the tests pin the runtime half with forged payloads in every field of every event. It governs this pipeline only: /search?q= is a URL, and the hosting platform's request logs record URLs (docs/data-flow-record.md). A count bounded by the catalogue size is still a number a forger chooses — it cannot carry an identifier, but it can carry noise.

controls.claims: a visitor who allowed measurement can withdraw from any page — 'Measurement preferences' in the footer, and on /privacy, reopens the consent prompt showing the current answer — and after Decline the next page sends nothing to /api/analytics
controls.knownLimit: Withdrawal stops future records; it does not delete log lines already written while consent was granted, and the privacy page says so rather than implying otherwise. The browser test covers the footer path on the configured projects; the reopen logic is also pinned in src/tests/unit/analytics.test.ts. Whether the retention and lawful-basis cells in docs/data-flow-record.md are satisfied is the privacy owner's question, not this control's.

controls.claims: any commerce the live site serves is attributed only after identity is observed — whether apex and www serve one build, whether a host answers one path the same way cold and warm, whether the edge agrees with the deployment it names — from dated, hashed, build-identified responses read under a streaming byte cap that reports truncation
controls.knownLimit: HTTP only — cookies, storage and service workers are e2e/fresh-session.spec.ts's question. A Vercel-protected deployment URL (401) cannot be compared, so commerce on the edge with the deployment unobserved, or with no comparable commit or body, is `unevaluable` rather than guessed; a body longer than the 2 MB read cap is `unevaluable` unless commerce was found in what was read. The visible-price detector is a regex over stripped HTML, pinned both ways by fixtures and by a clean run over 35 prerendered pages; its coverage beyond those is unknown (ADR 007). Cold/warm variance can also be an ISR regeneration landing between the two passes, now that pages revalidate hourly. The external-retrieval input is a flag a human sets; nothing measures it. The purchase-era copy it records is never part of the classification.

controls.claims: every non-clean or unevaluable live-surface classification opens or updates one issue with a deadline; an /ack from an owner, member or collaborator is required within 72h, the CODEOWNERS humans are mentioned exactly once when it is missed, a changed finding restarts the clock, and a clean report closes the issue
controls.knownLimit: Runs only where control-audit.yml runs — the default branch, on its schedule — so it does nothing until this lands on main. An acknowledgement records that a person has seen the finding, not that it is fixed; the issue stays open until the report is clean. Only the first 100 comments are read for an /ack. A probe that produced no JSON says nothing here; the step's own outcome reports that.

controls.claims: GitHub refuses to merge a known-bad pull request into main, proven by reading mergeability and the failing required check rather than by attempting the merge — and attributed to that check only when the canary is read as not a draft, free of conflicts, not behind its base, and the test merge commit does not disagree with the head
controls.knownLimit: A one-off proof, run by hand against a canary pull request: it proves the gate held at that moment for that head commit, not afterwards — probe-branch-protection.mjs is what keeps asking. It trusts GitHub's mergeable_state as the definition of 'would be refused', and since 2026-09-27 rules out the other causes of 'blocked' by separate readings (draft, mergeable, behind_by), because GitHub reported a draft PR as 'clean'. E2E is skipped on a canary whose verify fails (needs: verify) and GitHub counts that skip as satisfied, so the denial rests on the verify context alone. It cannot merge by construction (one GET-only helper, statically asserted by its test), so it cannot show the refusal message a person would see.
controls.humanAction: Re-run docs/runbooks/main-ruleset.md step 3 after any change to ruleset 24077858 (its updated_at moves), with the owner's explicit permission to push a canary branch: a v2 canary, ready for review, never merged, closed unmerged whatever the verdict. Never press merge on the canary: main auto-deploys to production.
controls.acceptedWhy: Restated 2026-10-03, after the proof ran. Canary #94 read NOT-DENIED on 2026-10-02 and was then merged, turning main red. At 07:56 UTC on 2026-10-03 the v2 canary #98 read `denied` (`required-context-unmet`, on the verify context alone): not a draft, no conflicts, 0 behind, head and test-merge commit in agreement, verify passing on the base, then closed unmerged (docs/runbooks/main-ruleset.md, Evidence). It moves the masterplan's githubGate flag to proven. It stays `not-configured` here on purpose: in this registry `configured` means a probe runs on its own, and this one runs by hand with the owner's permission (control-registry.test.ts; ADR 006). Calling a one-off proof configured would claim a watcher that does not exist. The continuing question belongs to merge-gate's probe.

controls.claims: production aliases go only to a commit whose own CI run explicitly passed verify and E2E (and, on a pull request, dependency scope); a skipped, cancelled or missing result is never read as a pass
controls.knownLimit: The check runs on every CI run and its verdict is exhaustively unit-tested, but it gates nothing on its own: until Vercel is told to wait for it, a red Production admission sits beside a deployment that takes the aliases anyway, which is what happened twice on 2026-10-02. Once Vercel waits for it, six limits remain. (1) A person with promote rights can Force Promote past a failing check, so it governs the automatic path, not people. (2) It holds the custom production domains (the apex and www); the deployment's own URL is still created and reachable. (3) It judges only its own run: merge_group and pushes to any other branch are refused by policy, not evaluated, and its failing path on a push to main is unit-tested only, because no bad commit is manufactured on main to observe it. (4) A failing check on a custom environment is a configuration rehearsal, not proof for production. (5) always() makes the job eligible to run after failed or skipped prerequisites, and no more: a cancelled run, a workflow that never triggers, a runner failure, or a missing or colliding check name can each leave no verdict, and each is a separate observation. Vercel also creates the production build before its deployment check decides alias assignment. Observed in real runs: the passing path on pull requests (#97, from run 37090486106) and on main's push (run 37099187496, `ADMITTED (push-main)`, 2026-10-03), and the failing path on a pull request (canary #98, run 37107871838, `REFUSED (pull_request)`). The failing path on main's push is not observed. (6) The verdict runs a script from the tree it judges: on a pull request the ruleset's own required checks still bind, but once merged that script governs main's push runs, which is why both admission scripts are in .github/CODEOWNERS. Its status moves only on the evidence named in docs/runbooks/production-admission.md.
controls.humanAction: Follow docs/runbooks/production-admission.md: in Vercel's project settings confirm the Git integration and automatic production aliasing, add a deployment check on the GitHub check `Production admission` that blocks production alias assignment (it is read on the deployment's commit SHA), and restrict and record who can Force Promote. Then record, dated, the main push run showing the check, and Vercel's check list read back. Proof beyond configuration needs an owner-approved negative test on the real promotion path that keeps the last good aliases; never manufacture a bad commit on main for it.
controls.acceptedWhy: Accepted 2026-10-03, the day after incident PR-94, when two READY production deployments were built from a main whose verify had failed. The repository half exists from this change: a check that passes only on explicit success. The other half is a Vercel project setting nobody in CI can make, so the gap is accepted, dated and escalated by probe-accepted-gap.mjs when it goes stale, rather than claimed as closed because a job turned green.

controls.claims: every file that defines the commerce boundary, the control registry or the deploy configuration has a named owner, and every ownership rule matches a tracked file
controls.knownLimit: Ownership requests a review; it does not block one. Required code-owner review deadlocks a one-maintainer repository — GitHub blocks self-approval — so it stays off until a second human reviewer exists. Rules are held to root-anchored, glob-free paths so matching has one answer; the matcher does not implement GitHub's full gitignore grammar.

controls.claims: docs/safety.md lists exactly the paths gate.yaml denies to an unattended loop
controls.knownLimit: Compares the two lists, not their effect: it cannot tell whether the loop actually honours gate.yaml. The prose list omitted vercel.json for a month before this existed.

controls.claims: a health, skin, imaging, regulatory, corrosion or durability claim renders its proposed wording only when a named reviewer has approved it, the approval is current, and a cited document covers the thing described; otherwise it renders its neutral fallback
controls.knownLimit: It governs claims that arrive as registry records; a claim written straight into copy never reaches the resolver, which is claim-lexicon's job. Expiry changes what renders and never fails a build (ADR 029). What renders reaches visitors within CLAIM_WITHDRAWAL_BOUND_SECONDS (3600) plus the one stale request that triggers regeneration: until 2026-09-27 every page was prerendered with no revalidation, and scripts/experiment-claim-expiry.mjs measured an approval two days past expiry still served on 8 cache HITs out of 8 at 228fdaf. That experiment is manual and re-run when the rendering mode or Next's major version changes; claim-expiry.test.ts holds the revalidate literals to the bound on every PR. No reviewer is reminded before an approval lapses (claimsNearingExpiry() has no scheduled caller) — a precondition of the first approval, since none exists. Evidence is a document reference and a reviewer's name; nothing verifies the document says what the reviewer recorded. Under the owner's 'enforce now' decision (2026-09-25) every record is pending, so today it proves the fallback path and, by fixture, the approved path.

controls.claims: no rendered page, component, config constant, metadata field or catalogue record states a health, skin, imaging, regulatory or corrosion claim outside an approved claim's exact wording
controls.knownLimit: A word list, so its coverage is a floor (ADR 007): each term is generalised from wording that was live on the site, and a claim in words nobody has used yet passes. Rendered checks cover the pages the test imports; the source scan covers src/app, src/components, src/config and src/lib/data, and in src/content only rendered fields. Text reached at runtime from outside those, or split across elements inside a word, is invisible.

controls.claims: commercial terms of sale (free shipping, returns, refunds, warranty, dispatch and delivery times, a purchase route) change only with a WS-H legal-review decision, and appear on no surface outside the pages that hold them
controls.knownLimit: It counts; it does not judge. A reworded term that keeps every count equal passes, and a term phrased outside its patterns is invisible. /privacy and the API routes are excluded from containment by stated reason. The pins record the text as it stood on 2026-09-26; whether any of it is lawful or still honoured is the adviser's question, not this test's.

controls.claims: nothing the contract forbids reaches the build output: no commerce identifier or forbidden host in any client asset, no absolute-scope identifier or credential-shaped value anywhere, and vendor residue in server output only where a registered WS-F route compiles it
controls.knownLimit: It reads what `next build` emitted on the runner, and PR builds restore .next/cache; builds on main run cold, so the deployed commit's artifact is always scanned from a clean build. It judges text: a value assembled at runtime from fragments, or fetched rather than bundled, is invisible to it — that is the egress controls' question. The staged-residue allowance is derived from the register's WS-F rows and the build's own chunk graph, so it shrinks to nothing on the day the webhook route is deleted. A matched credential-shaped value is reported by identifier, file and offset, never printed.

controls.claims: no page in any E2E journey requests an origin outside contract §12's browser allowlist or any §13 host, and none triggers a Content-Security-Policy violation
controls.knownLimit: It sees what the specs visit, through context.on('request'); a request the CSP blocks never reaches that listener, which is why violations are collected separately. Coverage is the union of the journeys the specs take, not every reachable page state. e2e-fixture-boundary.test.ts fails any spec that imports `test` from @playwright/test directly, so a new spec cannot step outside the fixture.

controls.claims: the API route handlers reach only contract §12's server allowlist — the mail provider and the rate-limit store — and nothing in §13
controls.knownLimit: It sees only globalThis.fetch: a handler that opened a raw socket, or an SDK that brought its own HTTP client, would be invisible. The SDKs are deliberately not mocked — a mocked SDK never calls fetch and the test would pass on an empty list — and two anti-vacuity assertions prove the stub is in their path. The webhook route is not exercised: it answers only an HMAC-signed delivery, makes no outbound call, and goes with WS-F.

controls.claims: every response carries a Content-Security-Policy whose connect-src is exactly 'self', with no forbidden host in any directive and no 'unsafe-eval'
controls.knownLimit: script-src and style-src keep 'unsafe-inline': a nonce would force every page to render dynamically and give up static generation, so the policy's strength is in connect-src, object-src, base-uri and frame-ancestors rather than in script origins. The Vercel preview toolbar (vercel.live) is blocked on previews, deliberately.

controls.claims: every retired commerce URL answers its contract §7 status and location for GET and HEAD, with and without a trailing slash, an encoded segment or a query string, asserted by status code without following redirects — and a stale action (POST in five encodings) on a 308 path, followed hop by hop, ends on that family's 410 page, never on a framework 404/405 or a page that implies it worked
controls.knownLimit: The variants are generated from §7, so a route family missing from the contract is missing from the matrix too — commerce-route-inventory.test.ts reconciles §7 against the filesystem and calls each retiredRoute() handler to close that. Concrete examples stand in for each `:path*` family; an exotic path shape no example resembles is not exercised. Since 2026-09-27 the 308 families are route handlers rather than next.config.ts redirects (a config redirect answers every method with the 308), so a legacy GET invokes a function where it used to match an edge rule. The 308 carries s-maxage=86400, so the edge answers repeats; the residual cost is about one invocation per legacy path per day.

controls.claims: a visitor who opens every approved page leaves with no cookie, no sessionStorage, no service worker, no Cache Storage and no IndexedDB, and with at most the one consent key in localStorage — and only after answering the banner
controls.knownLimit: It covers the journeys the spec takes on the two configured browser projects; storage written by a flow it does not exercise is not seen. The contact form's positive control stubs /api/contact, so it proves the form still submits, not that mail is delivered — contact-send-honesty and server-egress-boundary cover the server half.

$decisionAdrsComment: Every ADR is classified: it either describes a control (and appears as an `adr` above) or
it records a decision (and appears here with the reason it is not a control).
There is no third option, because 'unclassified' is how --sage shipped as 9-13px text at
1.97:1 in four places, and how a gate nothing enforced was asserted by five documents.
A control, for this purpose, is a mechanism whose absence is not visible from the thing it
protects. A decision is reasoning that is wrong out loud when violated.

decisionAdrs.docs/adr/048-the-name-keeps-its-own-face: The owner's rulings of 2026-10-04: the logo's background transparent wherever a platform can show it, Songmont a reference rather than a template, and the brand name in its original face. Decisions whose mechanisms are tests, not controls: brand-mark-asset (files), visual-assets (decoded bytes), typography-weights (the brand token bounded to the logotype), font-files and glyph-coverage.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/046-a-resolved-conflict-is-a-wr: Records the second lockfile incident (PR #101, ed7594a, 2026-10-03: all 22 conflict hunks resolved by keeping both sides) and corrects ADR 031's account of the first, which replays as a 7-hunk conflict rather than a clean merge. Its decisions are mechanisms already classified elsewhere: the lockfile half of the manifest-integrity control (whose `adr` remains ADR 031) and `.gitattributes`, whose behaviour that control's test asserts by a real merge.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/037-a-reconciliation-at-the-wro: A rule about the grain at which a reconciliation compares: a table parsed and reduced to a key before comparing has thrown away the columns it was meant to check. Its mechanism is the commerce-elimination-boundary control, which ADR 036 already classifies; this records why that control compares identifier sets rather than paths, and why a lexer that hides findings is erring in the unsafe direction.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/001-two-webhook-secrets.md: Records which of two secrets Shopify signs with. A fact about an external system, not a mechanism that can go missing.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/002-cart-completion-discriminat: A code-level discriminator. Its absence is a failing test, not a silent one.
A module boundary. Violating it is a lint or type error at the point of violation.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/004-static-fallback-is-not-a-da: An architectural rule. Its enforcement mechanism is the premise-detectors control above.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/005-english-only-storefront.md: A scope decision, watched by the premise-detectors control rather than being one.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/007-regex-guardrails-have-unkno: A rule about how controls are written, not a control. It constrains the entries above.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/009-api-version-must-be-asserte: Asserted inside verify-production.mjs, which the premise-detectors and smoke-liveness controls already cover.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/012-an-unassigned-escalation-is: An escalation convention for humans. Covered mechanically by the smoke-escalation control above.
A palette decision. Its enforcement is design-tokens-contrast.test.ts, which fails loudly in the gate.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/018-a-claim-about-a-control-is-: The rule this registry implements. It is the frame, not an entry in it.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/021-a-metric-with-only-one-dire: A rule about how sizes are written, and the audit that enforces it runs in the fast gate and fails by name. Its absence would be visible, which is what makes it a guardrail rather than a control.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/019-an-unclassified-entry-is-an: A rule about how enumerations are written, like ADR 007 is about how guardrails are written. Its three reconciliation tests run in the fast gate and fail by name, so their absence would be visible; that is what makes them guardrails rather than controls.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/023-the-last-link-is-a-person.m: States where the verification regress terminates. It is the frame the backstop field implements, not an entry in it — and its enforcement is a registry test that fails loudly in the fast gate.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/024-a-tool-never-pointed-at-a-k: A rule about how verification tools are built and admitted to this registry. Like ADR 007, it constrains the entries rather than being one.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/025-a-number-in-prose-is-a-clai: A rule about how documentation is written. Its reconciler runs in the fast gate and fails by name, so its absence would be visible — a guardrail, not a control.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/033-a-premise-that-expired-mid-: A rule about when a monitor must report a transition rather than a level, and about where an expired premise is repaired — at the evidence, not at the assumption. It refines the smoke-liveness control rather than adding one: the `stopped` verdict lives in that control's existing probe, its claims line now says so, and a second entry naming the same probe would be two answers to one question. Its enforcement is smoke-liveness.test.ts, eight assertions shown to fail against three mutations, which fail by name in the fast gate.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/028-a-fixture-is-the-input-you-: A rule about how verification tools are tested before being relied upon, like ADR 007 is about how guardrails are written and ADR 024 about pointing them at a known answer. It constrains the entries rather than being one, and its enforcement is parser-fuzz.test.ts, which fails by name in the fast gate.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/035-a-control-outlives-its-subj: A rule about what to do with a control when the thing it measures is deleted: re-found it, suspend it behind a premise detector that fails when the conditions return, or delete it and record the removal where the claim was — never narrow it to keep it green. Like ADR 007 (how guardrails are written), ADR 024 (pointing them at a known answer) and ADR 028 (testing them before relying on them), it constrains the entries in this registry rather than being one. Its enforcement is the premise detector the ADR itself installs: cache-tag-contract.test.ts asserts that nothing registers a cache tag and names, by name, the two suspended assertions that must be restored the moment anything does. That runs in the fast gate and fails loudly, which is what makes this a guardrail rather than a control.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/038-what-a-control-observes-is-: A rule about how a control states and proves what it observes: its knownLimit names the grain it observes, a fix starts from a falsifying example run against the real artifact, an instrument must FAIL the known-bad and PASS the known-good before its verdict counts, and attribution reads a recorded observation. Like ADR 024 it constrains the entries in this registry rather than being one; its enforcement is the sentinels added with it (retired-action-gone, bounded-response-read, live-surface-identity-before-cause, live-surface-ack-standing, denial-preconditions, claim-withdrawal-bound, consent-withdrawal), each seen red before it was registered, and claim-expiry.test.ts's check that the experiment's clock moves the clock the cache reads.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/040-seven-beats-one-strip.md: A homepage composition decision, not a control: it records that the page renders seven beats with one product strip and one dark interruption, and why. Its enforcement is the sequence pinned in homepage-composition-contract.test.ts and e2e/homepage-composition.spec.ts, and it is provisional until the owner confirms seven beats over eight.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/041-a-transparent-logo-is-a-mea: A brand-asset and naming decision, not a control: it records why every served copy of the knot mark is derived from one master with its black matte removed, why the brand name is one constant with a separate legal-entity name, and the owner's choices of silver, the 360px mark-only breakpoint and tiled icons. Its enforcement is in-repo and loud — brand-mark-asset.test.ts, brand-name.test.ts, header-fit.spec.ts and visual-assets.spec.ts — so its absence would be a red build, not a silent one.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/042-a-page-measured-before-it-a: A test-harness decision, not a control: settle() waits for streamed segments to be revealed and offendersPastViewport refuses a root with no box. Removing either is loud rather than silent — the brand-lockup probe and the no-box guard both throw on the unrevealed frame — so a regression shows up as a red e2e run instead of a vacuous pass.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/043-one-family-and-the-case-it-: A typography decision, not a control: one self-hosted family for every role, read from its own font tables, with headings and names set in their written case at declared weights. Its enforcement is in-repo and loud — typography-weights.test.ts, font-files.test.ts and glyph-coverage.spec.ts — so a mislabelled weight, a missing glyph, a forced capital or a face that fails to load is a red build, not a silent one.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/044-decided-from-the-language-n: A design decision, not a control: the Latin font, the 3:4 listing crop and the header are decided from the verified Songmont language and recorded as decisions rather than measurements. Its enforcement is in-repo and loud — design-consistency.test.ts holds the listing crop token and the homepage tile crops to one value and layout-invariants.spec.ts measures cards against the token — so a drift is a red build, not a silent one.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/045-a-form-is-a-request-from-an: A security and robustness decision, not a control: the contact route refuses cross-site requests and accepts a no-JavaScript form post, the search page reduces a repeated parameter to one string, Next.js is patched, and the width sweep becomes a spec. Its enforcement is in-repo and loud — api-contact-route.test.ts, search-param.test.ts, contact.spec.ts, navigation.spec.ts and responsive-sweep.spec.ts, with two sentinels proving the unit guards can fail — so a regression is a red build, not a silent one.
decisionAdrs.docs/adr/026-a-capability-is-not-a-verdi: A rule about how a control decides whether it may run: gate on what a check needs, not on whether the whole setup is valid. Its enforcement is preflight-secrets.test.ts and the workflow's own conditions, which fail loudly in the fast gate.

$backstopComment: Every control names what catches ITS OWN failure, and following the chain must end at a person.
`control:<id>` points at another entry. `human:<cadence>` is the floor. There is no third form,
and a cycle is a failure: two controls backstopping each other is a chain with no bottom.
This exists because the bottom rung broke on arrival. control-audit.yml — the tier that watches
every other control — was invalid YAML from the commit that created it and produced three runs
with zero jobs. Nothing in this repository noticed. A human reading the Actions tab did.
ADR 022 conceded the audit cannot detect its own death and left it there. This says where the
regress stops instead: docs/weekly-verification.md, five minutes, once a week, regardless of what
any dashboard says — because the premise is that the dashboards may be lying.
$acceptedComment: A `not-configured` control names when its gap was accepted and why.
probe-branch-protection.mjs exits 0 while the registry honestly says not-configured, so an
accepted gap raises no alarm — correctly, since a six-hourly alarm about a state only a human can
change is the channel ADR 011 says people learn to mute.
But silence has its own failure: `accepted` decays into `forgotten`, and nothing marks the moment.
So the acceptance expires instead of the alarm firing. control-registry.test.ts fails when an
acceptance is older than ACCEPTED_GAP_MAX_AGE_DAYS, which forces a person to restate it or close
it — once, in a diff a reviewer sees, rather than every six hours in a channel nobody reads.
